speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ACTION BY GOVERNMENT TO SUPPLY DRUGS TO THOSE UNABLE TO PAY FOR THEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the comments of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton), the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) and the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard). I would like to deal with the questions raised by those hon. members and, more specifically, with the motion now before us.
Motion No. 6 in the name of the hon. member for Oxford deals with a very specific question. In effect, it recommends that the government give consideration to providing a form of care to those who are unable to care for themselves. In his speech, the hon. member paid particular attention to those over 65. I would like to say that as a federal government we do not have full and total jurisdiction in this particular case. Under the Canada Assistance Plan which was passed by parliament, the federal government has provided a vehicle in fact to achieve the objectives of this motion. Under the Canada Assistance Plan we pay 50 per cent and the province pays 50 per cent to look after those in need. That includes the elderly and those of any other age group which needs medicines or drugs.
The provinces have the responsibility of administering that program. This means that I, at this moment, cannot really see any point in passing the recommendation presently before the House. However, the comments of hon. members certainly lead me to believe there is need for further consideration to be given to the whole question of pharmacare and the approach toward the provision of free drugs to those in need.
I would like to comment now on some of the remarks of the hon. member for Assiniboia. He is really advocating a universal pharmacare program. This is something which I agree has to be considered by the provinces and by the federal government. As hon. members know, a federal-provincial conference of health ministers is to be held in the near future, at which the provincial health ministers, along with the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare, will be giving consideration to a whole new formula designed to look after health care costs. Hopefully, an agreement will be reached which will allow the provinces a full range of programs which they themselves can initiate without in any way jeopardizing the cost-sharing arrangements with the federal government. At present there is a 50-50 cost-sharing formula, depending on the kind of service which is provided. This means that in many cases provinces confine their medicare operations to areas which are more expensive than others because we share the costs with them.
Under the formula which is proposed, financing will be on a per capita basis and the provinces will have full and complete freedom to involve themselves in a whole broad range of medicare facilities. This will, it is hoped, cut down the rapid escalation in health care costs as well as provide better health care delivery systems in the prov-
April 2, 1973

inces. It is my opinion that such a conference is the kind of forum at which the question of pharmacare costs should be raised. I believe that many members of this House as well as many Canadians in general recognize the problems and the benefits which may result from a universal pharmacare program. I am hopeful that the conference of health ministers will take this question into consideration very seriously.
In addition to the forthcoming conference of health ministers, a further conference has been arranged to consider the Canada Assistance Plan and a whole series of welfare programs now operating in Canada, whether federally initiated or provincially applied and initiated. The one thing we have asked all the ministers to bear in mind during the initial discussions on welfare problems in Canada is that they should set aside for the time being questions of jurisdiction so that they can look at the whole problem and develop a formula which will benefit all Canadians. We could then zero in, determine who is responsible for what, and how the programs would be implemented. It is hoped that the result of such an approach would be to provide better welfare services in Canada, better programs which would reduce the amount of red tape, giving Canadians easier access to the kinds of assistance which are really necessary.
As has been mentioned many times in this House, the Speech from the Throne referred to the provision of a guaranteed annual income to those who are unable to work, and undertook to provide some other assistance to those who are able to work but who cannot find jobs. Certain of those who are in need in that group-and there are many of them; the handicapped, for example-could well be classified as unable to work, yet at the same time there may be many handicapped people who think it is in their interest to work, that it would be good for them if they did so. This is the kind of question which has to be resolved. I am hopeful that in the over-all review which will next take place during Easter week, the kinds of representations made here today will form part of that consideration.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 COMMUNICATIONS BELL CANADA-RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion was placed before the House, not as a gesture but because I believe it is important for the people of Canada, for the minister and for the government to have the views of Members of Parliament as it considers this important issue and tries to arrive at a decision. The first fact I want to underline-and I shall go from one point to another as quickly as I can-is that Bell Canada has been given four increases in three and a half years. They had an increase on September 25, 1969, another on December 1, 1970, a third on May 19, 1972, and a fourth on March 27, 1973. Each time, the Canadian Transport Commission gave Bell Canada not always all it requested, but almost all.
What disturbs me even more is that the increase approved last Friday by the Canadian Transport Commission is merely a prelude to application B which is already before the Canadian Transport Commission, and if that were granted the increases would make those approved last Friday pretty small potatoes. Obviously, Bell Canada is seeking more and more of its customers' money. I say, Mr. Speaker, it is time to call a halt to the monopolistic gouging by Bell Canada of the people of Canada.
The second point I make, Mr. Speaker, is that Bell Canada is not claiming that it needs these increases for profit or for its operations; Bell Canada is claiming it needs them in order to have capital for further investment. What it will do is get from its customers a pool of investment capital for which it does not have to pay, and I say that a company as powerful as Bell should not be allowed to tax its customers; and that is what its rate increases really mean.
Mr. Speaker, what is this poor, poverty stricken company about? What have its profits been? I received only

today the annual report of Bell Canada for the year 1972, and on one of the pages of that report there are financial figures for 1963 to 1972 inclusive, that is, over a period of ten years. During that period there was a steady and large increase in profits every year except one: in 1969, the profits were slightly below those of 1968. But to make up for it, in 1970 there was an increase of 17.2 per cent over 1969; in 1971 and increase of 10.5 per cent over 1970; in 1972 an increase of 11.9 per cent over 1971.
Mr. Speaker, when you look at the profit picture of Bell Canada in these ten years, you find that from $68.25 million of profit in 1963, this gouging company reached a profit of $164.75 million in 1972. How much more does Bell Canada want out of the people of this country? And I am not talking about gross profit before taxes; I am talking about profit after taxes that are currently paid, which include deferred taxes in large amount. In addition to these profits, according to this report which I have just studied, Bell Canada now controls ten other companies outright and has an interest, although not a controlling interest, in several others.
I say that the people of Canada have already made a sufficient investment in Bell Canada. Some hon. members may not know this, but I have been interested in the subject and as at the end of 1971, Bell Canada had total deferred taxes of $224 million. By the end of 1972, these deferred taxes amounted to $322 million. That represents an interest-free loan by the people of Canada to this huge corporation of $322 million at the end of 1972.
What is even more significant in respect of Bell Canada's request for an increase is that one of the ways it can add to its deferred tax position is to continue to invest and to change its machinery and equipment. The more it changes its equipment every year, the fancier the telephone, the more it is able to avoid paying taxes by deferring them. That is the only way a corporation can do this, by continuing to buy new equipment and machinery; only then can they take advantage of the deferred tax provisions of our unfair tax system. The amount of $322 million from the people of Canada is more than enough to give to this huge, powerful corporation.
It is for these reasons, and because these facts seem to be overwhelmingly persuasive, that I think Bell Canada ought not to be allowed any more increases at the expense of its customers, the majority of the people of this country. On this basis I placed this motion on the order paper.
I want now to turn the attention of the minister to the act and its relevant section. It is, of course, true that parliament gave, under the National Transportation Act- as it had previously given under the Railway Act-the first responsibility for regulating these prices, tariffs and charges to the Canadian Transport Commission. I have very grave doubt whether the Canadian Transport Commission is equipped to deal with this matter, whether it is equipped to understand the importance of the material that Bell Canada places before the commission every time it asks for a rate increase. Therefore, I have very grave doubt whether the commission is in fact protecting the public interest.
April 2, 1973

I note with sadness that the president of the commission which granted this increase to Bell Canada is the Hon. Edgar Benson, former minister of finance. Whatever one may say about the Canadian Transport Commission, I plead with the minister and members of the government to realize that the ultimate responsibility for protecting the public interest lies with them. The act places that responsibility upon them. Section 64(1) of the National Transportation Act reads in part as follows:
The governor in council may at any time, in his discretion-
Let me point out this is not in the discretion of the Canadian Transport Commission; it is in the discretion of the governor in council. It continues:
-either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the commission, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order that the governor in council may make with respect thereto is binding upon the commission and upon all parties.
There could not be more clear language. The act in fact says, I suggest, that the initial responsibility for regulating these rules lies with the Canadian Transport Commission, but that the ultimate responsibility for protecting the public interest is placed on the government of Canada by the section of the act to which I have just referred. I plead with the government not to abrogate its responsibility in this case. I plead with the minister and the government to carry out its duty under the section I have read, because there is no reason for this increase.
I appreciate, as I indicated by a question this afternoon and as I indicated to the minister in conversation on the subject this morning, that it would take time for the government to make a final decision. I hope it will be a decision to rescind this unconscionable increase in rates which the CTC has thoughtlessly given Bell Canada. I appreciate this will take time. The government cannot easily do something about a decision of a body given the power under the act. The government needs to have a full study made, not only of the decision but of all the material that was placed before the commission, so it can justify whatever decision it will make.
Because I appreciate that, I suggested to the minister in my question this afternoon and in my conversation with him this morning that the government ought to immediately suspend the application of the CTC decision pending a final decision of the government on the order made by the commission. If the government takes a week or two to make its decision, by that time the new tariffs will be in effect and I suggest at that point the government will be caught and will not able to act where it might easily want to act after studying the decision and all the relevant material.
It seems to me there is clearly a prima facie case to question the action of the CTC. It seems there is clearly an initial reason for wanting time to study the material, in order to act upon it in accordance with the authority given the governor in council by the section of the act I have read. In order to give itself the time necessary, I see no reason in the world why the governor in council could not, within the next week or so, make a decision to suspend
Bell Canada
the application of the order of the Canadian Transport Commission pending further study of the entire matter.
The CTC has obviously been intimidated by this large corporation I submit that the government must not permit itself to be intimidated by this huge, monopolistic corporation in Canada. I suggest, also, that it is time we served the interests of the people of Canada instead of the interests of Bell Canada. As I said earlier, the time has long passed when a halt should be called to this constant demand by Bell Canada for more and more from its customers, the people of this country. Now is the time for the government to act along the lines I have suggested.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), I do not intend to plead on behalf of this party for relief by the government. It has been our task, which has proved to be ineffective, to plead with the government in respect of other issues. Our efforts in this regard have proved that the government is insensitive, not only to the pleas of the opposition but to the pleas of the public.
The recent approval by the CTC of the application by Bell Canada for rate increases is yet another example of the contradictory and convoluted non-policy of the government with regard to combating inflation. In the February 19 budget address, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) adamantly claimed that the 1973 budget was designed to reduce inflationary pressures in Canada and to offset the effects of past inflation. He implored business, labour and the professions to "exercise price and income restraint". Yet the Liberal government has failed to offer any specific guidelines or policy proposals to implement and enforce their budget goodies. The increases allowed Bell Canada, and others under the CTC's jurisdiction, are so large and out of proportion that there can be no relationship whatsoever to any reasonable price guidelines as advocated in the February 19 budget speech.
I find it interesting that there was placed on our desks a short while ago a green document from which I should like to quote a small portion which I find very interesting. It reads:
The present federal regulatory body for telecommunications carriers is the Canadian Transport Commission (CTC) which derives its authority from the National Transportation Act, the Railway Act, and the special acts of incorporation of the undertakings subject to its authority. The CTC either does not have, or has not in the past exercised, authority over a number of matters that are dealt with in subsection C below.
The powers of the CTC are suitable only for the broad economic regulation of a particular corporate entity and are not related to any statutory national policy and objectives-
I repeat the words "are not related to any statutory national policy and objectives."
__such as the vital importance of east/west communications to the
sovereignty and economic prosperity of Canada, and to the preservation of its social and cultural identity.
It goes on to say that the recent criteria for the exercise of regulatory authority require the commission to ensure that questions in respect of tolls shall not subject any particular person or company or any particular description of traffic to any undue or unreasonable prejudice or

I stand corrected, Mr. Speaker. I was directing attention to a question asked by the Leader of the Opposition about wholesale price increases and the government's intention to implement new measures to control inflation. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) replied:
I have no policy statement to announce today on that matter.
We have had no policy statement since then having to do with the control of price increases. The day after the budget was presented, with the plea of the finance minister to business, the government's spending estimates were introduced for the fiscal year 1973-74. These showed an increase of almost 15 per cent over the previous fiscal year.
We would strongly recommend that the government take advantage of the power vested in it by law and review the decision of the CTC to increase rates for Bell Canada. One of the facts I find so interesting is that originally, as I understand it, the CTC was developed to protect the consumers' interest; in other words, to defend the public from increases by bodies which had powers unaffected by the normal question of competitive rates.
I recall an occasion many years ago, while I was mayor of a small city, when the Association of Mayors and Reeves decided to object to similar rate increases, however, the association did not have the financial base upon which to argue in respect of the decision of the CTC to give Bell Canada an increase. When the provinces object to such increases, frequently they have difficulty in finding sufficient money in their budgets to oppose an increase, simply because Bell Canada with its army of lawyers, economists, and so on, is extremely well prepared and well financed to fight such a battle.
I suggest that this applies not only to the CTC in respect of Bell Canada but also to freight rates, telecommunication and transmission rates which the CTC also controls. So far as that goes, we have the present government not using the authority it has to hold in check other regulatory bodies, such as the National Energy Board, the CRTC, and others. These bodies, seemingly, grant increases whenever asked and the government does not provide an opportunity for the public as a whole to object to the increases.
Corporate law is becoming very complex and the individual Canadian is not equipped to appear before the

CTC and present his views in a manner that could overcome the rhetoric of the legal staff of Bell Canada or other large bodies. So we find that the government has increased its spending and is allowing its own regulatory bodies to increase rates without any guidelines whatever. We feel the government must recognize the state of the economy for what it is and, furthermore, must introduce effective measures and guidelines to combat increasing inflation, particularly in areas under its jurisdiction.

I am sure the hon. member for York South thought of all Canadians this afternoom and specially of those who have a hard time making ends meet. Through this motion, he appeals to all, and particularly to those who are responsible for this Commission and have the power to authorize or refuse the increases requested by Bell Canada.

I thank the hon. member for calling me to order. I believe it means practically the same thing, if we went to the same school. We probably did not, but I believe we both speak French. And the terms are very similar.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote now from an article published in the Friday, February 16 issue of Le Soleil, by Mr. Burtnick, a representative of the Ontario government, who says he is shocked that Bell Canada, over at least six or seven years, has been requesting rate increases every year or two. And Bell Canada never fails to indicate that the request for increased rates is motivated by increased salaries. The low-wage earner is always blamed for the poor management of those who are seeking excuses for their mismanagement.
I should like to quote the statistics supplied to me by the Corporation of Quebec teachers, in a brief addressed to each hon. member, to prove to the House that salaries are not the cause of Bell Canada's increased operation costs. In 1966, Bell Canada had 40,008 employees and total salaries were $225,400,000; salary increases were $25,200,000, i.e. 12.6 per cent.
In 1967 the number of employees at Bell Canada was 38,123, salaries $236,800,000 and the growth in salaries $11,400,000, a 5 per cent increase.
In 1968 employees numbered 37,489, salaries reached $250,700,000 and the growth in salaries $13,900,000, a 5.9 per cent increase.
In 1969 it was clear that it was certainly not the rise in salaries that was behind the tariff increases, for Bell Canada had 38,686 employees, paid $274 million in salaries and the growth in salaries was $23,300,000, a 9.3 per cent increase.
In 1971, the company had 39,136 employees, the payroll was $333,800,000 and the growth in salaries was $31,900,000, a 10.6 per cent increase.
In 1973 the number of employees is 41,000, salaries amount to $398,800,000 and the growth in salaries is $30,200,000, an 8.2 per cent rise.
Bell Canada stressed to the Commission the cause of its tariff increases. I believe that if this company is granted the increase that it is now requesting, this will be the equivalent of disguised taxation which, once again, will come from the pocket of the small taxpayer.
Bell Canada attributes the rise in its operating costs to the following elements: the rise in prices, $11 million; increased taxation $12,900,000-we see that it is again the "behind the door" taxation which is putting the tariffs up-and the new collective agreement, $33,400,000.
The figures I quoted earlier show that the cost of the collective agreement, $33,400,000, is not the correct figure. I have worked out the average of the figures I quoted earlier; it comes to $26,600,000 and not $33,400,000. Therefore, it is no excuse for Bell Canada to say that it is the small salary earners who are lining their pockets, and that that is what is putting up the cost of its services.
Bell Canada
To quote again from the same newspaper; Le Soleil, Mr. D. W. Burtnick stresses:
Last year the company installed 177,000 more telephones than expected-at an average cost of $17.50-but in its end-of-year statement, Bell said it had spent $500,000 less than expected.
And it claims it is forced to put up its tariffs. If it sets up more equipment than anticipated on the other hand, it incurs less expenditures.
The quotation goes on as follows:
The Ontario representative also blamed those who, testifying for Bell, stated that if the company could not increase its rates, the service would deteriorate.
In the past, one had to travel 2 or 3 miles to find a phone in a home of a remote rural area. On the other hand, we find one in almost every house and even sometimes 3 or 4. I think that it shows that Bell Canada does not have to raise its rates to finance itself. Moreover, in order to show what is going on in Quebec, I would like to quote again Le Soleil:
Calyle Gilmour from Covey Hill recalled that Quebecers already pay $24 million to Bell and that the company will pay $32 million in school and municipal taxes in Ontario, but only $7.4 million in Quebec.
Once more, the people of Quebec are those who will bear the cost. In Ontario, Bell Canada almost always purchases its equipment from a company which it owns outright. If this company increases the prices of the equipment it sells, the user who must pay cannot be held responsible for it.
Statistics show that 99 per cent of families have a telephone and that Canadians are the world leaders as regards the use of the telephone, with 6.2 calls a day.
Therefore, I believe that the telephone can no longer be considered as a luxury but rather as a vital service for all the Canadian people. Consequently, anyone should be able to afford it. Even the government of Quebec considers as essentiel the cost of telephone when calculating the amount of the benefits to be paid to the 300,000 people who live on welfare in Quebec. I suggest it is very important for the government to see to it that this vital service is not too expensive.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to describe all the aspects of this rate increase, but I wish to emphasize the fact that Bell Canada is going much too far when establishing some rates which always go up every two or three years.
With this new application A there will be a 50 per cent increase for installing new telephones for anyone who is moving into a new house or who has no telephone. This is nonsense, Mr. Speaker.
Considering that there is a 50 per cent increase by set, if a homeowner has had 4 telephone sets installed, equipment charges for the four sets are increased by 50 per cent.
Moreover, if there are two or three telephones in a house, it makes no difference: so much is charged by set. Nor can I understand how it is costing to make a call from a Contempra phone than from a standard phone. There are a lot of anomalies in that rate increase and once again I congratulate the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) for having brought that motion in.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend in this debate to stand up for Bell Canada and its claims. Nor is it my intention to stand up for the decision made by CTC nor the commission itself, the very simple reason being that the decision was made exactly three and a half days ago and out of those three and a half days two were non-working days. I think that the opposition and my own colleagues would have every reason to find me extremely presumptuous and question the soundness of my remarks if I ventured to stand up for or condemn the decision when all hon. members of this House barely had time to peruse the document.
This is why I am somewhat surprised to see the opposition express its views in such a firm and categorical way when it is a document, as I say, that nobody has had time to examine in depth; if somebody did have time to do so in the period of time available to us the analytical faculties of that man would have to be proclaimed as those of a genius.
What I would like to deal with, Mr. Speaker, is the resolution addressed to the government urging it to act immediately by way of the exceptional powers which are found in the statutes and whose existence nobody in this House will deny, of course.
It is to this subject that I would like to devote most of my time tonight because this haste to tell the government: Cancel, suspend, rescind or modify this decision which you hardly had time to read, seems most suspect to say the least.
In this House and in this Parliament we have a tradition of which I would like to remind hon. members. The opposition has unduly often reminded us of this tradition over the few years I have been there. This tradition, which is the expression of Parliament's will, consists in requiring from the executive power that it respect the independance of constituted bodies, especially quasi-judicial bodies.
I say "especially" because the opposition has always been extremely touchy in the area of executive power interference even with bodies not of quasi-judicial nature. For instance, I am thinking about the charges or suspicions which have been expressed more than once when someone feared or pretended to fear that the government had tried to interfere with the decisions of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for instance, of the Canadian Radio-Television Commission or even of the Art Council.
The opposition has always shown paradoxical positions. On the one hand, they ask questions and urge the government to act, as the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) just did. They blame the government for its lack of action one and a half working days after the decision has been published and, on the other hand, with this splendid paradoxical position, if the government is so unfortunate as to voice one single critic against quasijudicial bodies, similar clamours arise from the opposition but this time in a reverse direction. They then tell the executive: Hands off; those are bodies whose freedom is extremely dear to this Parliament, whose independance has been established by Parliament and the government should not tamper with it. fMr. Beaudoin.]
I am surprised to hear shouting from that corner-I do not know where it came from exactly-because when I think, for example, about the protests at the slightest suspicion or at the least indication of governmental intervention in the administration of the Canada Council or the CBC, it is certainly, and I congratulate them, our friends from the New Democratic Party who tried the hardest to prevent an action of this type.

I do not know what the hon. member wants with his red herrings, Mr. Speaker, but if he only came back from fishing, we might go on with the discussion.
Actually, at the CRTC, for example-and I want to make it very clear-even though the government is authorized to issue guidelines to that agency, within certain limits set out in the act, to my knowledge, in four years and a half to five years it has done so only four times and those guidelines were all likely to gain the support of all members.
The first guideline, it will be remembered, was designed to bring back to Canada certain radio and television stations, and cablevision companies.
The purpose of the second was to force cablevision companies to reserve a channel for educational television and another for community television.
The third as applied to educational television, gave the provinces authority, if they themselves were creating independent corporations for this purpose, to hold broadcasting licences.
I am convinced that this tradition, this respect for the independence of commissions having quasi-legal status, for independent agencies created by this Parliament, is one from which Parliament has no intention to depart.
I shall now come to the second part of my argument to show hon. members how irregular it would be to force the government, and for the government to accept this constraint, to suspend, alter or reverse, a day and a half after its release, a decision following almost a month of public hearings and a month of deliberation by the Commission itself. And apparently we are being asked tonight to take, in two or three days, a decision which is per se, and I emphasize this point, an exceptional one. Because of course, upon reading the Act which contains the section which the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) read out a little while ago, it can be seen that this Act provides for very general acceptance, without amendment, of the Commission's decisions.
This power of the executive to suspend, amend or rescind decisions is obviously exceptional.
As I said this afternoon, when answering a question by the hon. member for York South, it would be quite unusual for the executive to use these powers unless such an intervention is justified by a very serious reason. I gave two examples which to me would be reasons-

First I gave the example of a decision which would mainly be based on an obviously false principle and, second that of a decision which would obviously be based on inaccurate facts or serious falsehoods.
Those are but two examples among many others. There might be other reasons as I said this afternoon during the oral questions period. I do not reject a government intervention, but I want to stress the point that it would not be made without very serious reasons. According to a practice in the Communications Department that has been going on ever since the department itself has been established, as soon as a decision is published, it is submitted to the high officials and advisors of the department so that it can be considered at length. They report to the minister who, although he may accept or reject their advice, must hear from them before rendering his decision: he must be aware of the pros and cons which could make the executive power, the governor in council act directly, use its reserved powers. This is a matter of routine.
Such a practice, I repeat, was resorted to as soon as the department was established and this is the first thing I did myself as soon as the ruling being considered tonight was published.
It would be irregular, I think, to expect such a study to be completed within a day and a half, within two, three or maybe five days, in view of the long process which enabled the Commission itself to reach the ruling that is the subject-matter of this resolution.
Such interference, as I said, constitutes an exceptional measure and there should be serious reasons for invoking powers reserved to the cabinet.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said in his statement that the CTC "was not equipped" to discharge the responsibilities entrusted to it. Mr. Speaker, the truth is-and the government probably knew it before being told by the opposition-that the circumstances have changed faster than the Commission could transform itself. And I should like to refer the hon. members who did not read it, to page 26 of the Green Book I had the honour of tabling recently in the House. The hon. members will realize that the government is quite aware of the problem to which the hon. member for York South referred, and that it is now clearly considering in that Green Book a reorganization of the Telecommunications Section of the CTC.
Incidentally, I should also like to tell the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) who, during the question period today, proposed that consumers should get help from the government, under some form or other, to
Bell Canada
submit their claims and make their case before the CTC, that if he refers to page 14 of the Green Book, he will see that this possibility is actually being considered. In fact, we are saying, and I quote:
The Government is accordingly considering a number of suggestions with regard to the representation of consumer interests when licensing and regulatory matters are being dealt with by the Minister of Communications and the federal regulatory bodies.
Therefore, in the government, we are quite aware of the fact that some changes are urgently needed in that respect, and Mr. Speaker, I should like to give the House the assurance that after having conducting the consultations called for by the Green Book, we intend to act and to act with determination and haste, in order to take the corrective measures required in a situation that we have fully looked into.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, here is the last point that I want to deal with. A short while ago when I talked of cancelling or changing a decision I heard someone: It is only a matter of suspension. So I think that the suspension-again I do not exclude the possibility of the government eventually taking this decision or of being myself compelled, once an analysis has been made by my department, to recommend to the government such a measure-of a decision by the Canadian Transport Commission already constitutes a kind of judgment made on the validity of the decision itself. And I was concerned, for instance, when I heard the hon. member for York South state positively that "the Board has been intimidated". He was certainly not making it easy for us to accept a suggestion that is his own, because after this charge has been made in such a positive manner, if we were going to suspend the decision we would now seem to admit that the Commission has been intimidated.

Mr. Speaker, as I suggested in my supplementary question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) earlier today, the motion before the House raises the ghosts of the past. This evening's debate has been held before. What is being said in the present debate is almost a repetition of what was said in the debates of 1966 and 1967 on the setting up of the Canadian Transport Commission. At that time, members of all parties worked together in this House as members of all parties have never before worked to produce the national transportation bill and to remove from the control of Parliament over 40 per cent of the economy of this nation. The House put that power into the hands of a commission, known as the Canadian Transport Commission, in the interests of efficiency in the running of this country.
In that debate those of us who were concerned about this tremendous transfer of power to the board issued warning after warning, as can be found in the speech of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) of December 12, 1966, and again in the speech of the hon. member for Peace River as well as in my own speech delivered on

April 2, 1973
Bell Canada
January 12, 1967. All the things I want to say tonight can be found in Hansard for those two days. What warning did we issue? We warned that one of the great dangers in turning all this tremendous power over to a board would be the risk of the acceptance of a principle of infallibility by this board that we had seen demonstrated in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, other boards, commissions and Crown corporations in this country. Those warnings of 1966-67 have come home to roost in this debate on the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission on the Bell rates.
It is absolutely impossible for the ordinary layman to be able to comprehend the technical aspects of a rate hearing and make his views known before the board on such matters. If you think there is difficulty in connection with Bell rate applications, think how difficult it is to understand the applications that will come from the railways in the years ahead.
Let me tell the House a little story based on the experience of 10 years ago in the MacPherson Royal Commission. One of the railway companies, Canadian Pacific Railways, has a study prepared on moving grain out of western Canada into the export market. Since there were no experts in Canada able to do this, they went to New York and got a reputable group of accountants to produce this study. The study showed that the railway operated at a tremendous loss in 1958 in the hauling of western grain to market. This alarmed the Western governments and wheat selling organizations in the west. They hired another group of experts from New York, equally reputable, to study the same figures. They proved conclusively, with the same figures, that this railway had made money carrying this grain to market. The royal commission had two reports before it, so they hired another group of experts, also from New York, to study the two reports. The third group published a volume three and one half inches in depth called the Third Volume of the MacPherson Report analysing these reports. They finally concluded there was a slight profit in the moving of grain.
This story is told for a purpose, mainly that the technical aspects of rate setting are beyond the comprehension of an ordinary person. Realizing this is 1966 and 1967, the hon. member for Peace River moved an amendment. This amendment laid down the best structure we could suggest for setting up a statutory committee, not under the control of the cabinet or the Prime Minister, but under the control of this House. The minute the House met, the statutory committee was to meet. This committee would have had at its disposal competent advisers who could cope with and examine the reports, provide us with a window on these hearings and translate them into language the laymen in the House of Commons could understand.
That amendment was turned down in 1967 and turned down in a committee vote. Every member of the Liberal government of that day voted against the amendment. Every member of the New Democratic Party also voted against it on the grounds that we should turn over complete power to these boards or Crown corporations and give them the power of infallibility. The first chairman was the Hon. Mr. Pickersgill, "Slick Pick". The next chairman is a Buddha called Benson. Do we have to get down

on our knees and say that this board is infallible? I have known these men for 25 years. They are just as awkward and stupid as I am, and they make just as many mistakes. When the Prime Minister stood up in this House today and said that this board was set up to handle all these things, he not only let down the power of parliament to have some say over such an important segment of our community and our economy, he abdicated his right as the head of a government to have some say.

speechtext:
My seat-mate, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker), pressed home the point this afternoon. I wish to quote from the act which was quoted by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). The act in question which guides this group called the Canadian Transport Commission states:
The Governor in Council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the Commission.
It is bad enough having parliament removed from the scene with no sophisticated committee able to handle these technical matters, but just imagine the position of the ordinary citizen of Canada appearing before a board on technical matters which are beyond the comprehension of almost every person in Canada, except the technically qualified men in accounting at this level. He has no chance at all. When I heard the Prime Minister today abdicating the right of parliament, I realized this was a complete acceptance of the principle of infallibility of government boards.
In my speech of 1967, I stated that I did not blame people who are socialistically oriented and believe in this sort of nonsense; that is their right. However, I believe that a government which calls itself Liberal should know better. A Tory who knows something about the defence of the human race should certainly know better. Our party voted to give and maintain some power for this House of Commons.
Infallibility of government boards? The Prime Minister is as bad as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), who last Friday over a television station in Regina and Saskatoon enunciated the same principle about the Canadian Wheat Board. Once you appoint these men to the board, they achieve infallibility. Even Pope John gave up the notion of infallibility 20 years ago. Here we have a government that accepts no responsibility.
I close my remarks by saying that what we are hearing here is a doctrine of elitism. We have in power a government, supported by a party on this side of the House, that believes it is perfectly right and proper for the representatives of the people to turn their power over to boards and give them complete power and right over our fortunes ever after. Elitism, infallibility or whatever you call it, it is not democracy. It is not democratic government in a modern corporate state like the one in which we live.

speechtext:
The resolution is not a criticism of the CTC. I believe all members of the House would like to repudiate some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain. The question here is the possibility of reconsideration on broader grounds of the decision the CTC has made. It is precisely because the CTC is limited by its statute in terms of what it can do that the problem to which the motion addresses itself has arisen.
The problem is in fact larger than the problem immediately at hand. First, there is the unfortunate inadequacy of the structure, inasmuch as jurisdiction over both transportation and communications has been joined in one regulatory body.
Bell Canada
At the time Canada came into being, the distinction between communications and transportation was scarcely realized. Certainly, it was not clearly realized.

speechtext: There is no difference.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 COMMUNICATIONS BELL CANADA-RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
The only reference to communications as a distinct subject in the British North America Act is in section 92(10)(a) in the mention of telegraphs. The other words in that subsection refer to "works and undertakings connecting a province with other provinces or extending beyond the limits of a province." It was to bring it under this category of "works and undertakings" that the act incorporating the Bell Telephone Company in 1880 was amended by a statute of 1882. In section 4 of that statute it was stated:
The said act of incorporation is hereby amended and the works thereunder authorized are hereby declared to be for the general advantage of Canada.
It was only under this type of provision in our constitution that federal regulatory jurisdiction over what we now consider to be distinctively communications began to emerge. Subsequently, with the decision of the Privy Council in the radio reference of 1932, it was recognized that here was a new field of regulation, and not long after that radio, and then television, began to be separately regulated. Telegraphs and telephones were left where they had begun, in the field of transportation, and I suggest this is no longer satisfactory in the year 1973.
The second inadequacy is a consequence of the first, and is an inadequacy in the terms of reference. The Railway Act stipulates that the Transport Commission regulate federally-chartered telecommunications common carriers and approve all rates for public and private wire communications. The type of regulation envisaged by this act is set out in section 321 (1):
All tolls shall be just and reasonable and shall always, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions with respect to all traffic of the same description carried over the same route, be charged equally to all persons at the same rate.
Mr. Speaker, these are not sufficient grounds of consideration today when we must respond to the type of request which is continually being placed before the Commission by Bell Canada. I should like again to draw the attention of the House to the fact that the minister, in a green paper, has himself suggested that a new body should be set up, one which we migh call a Canadian Communications Commission. This would separate, once and for all, the regulation of communications from the regulation of transportation.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 COMMUNICATIONS BELL CANADA-RATE INCREASES
speechtext: And how would that help?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 COMMUNICATIONS BELL CANADA-RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
It would have authority over all matters involving communication. This would leave us in a much better situation because all issues affecting communications would be dealt with together, and the regulatory body would be able to develop expertise in that particular field. The terms of reference drawn up for that Commission should, of course, be sufficiently broad as to enable it to take into account much wider considerations, when considering applications for rate increases, than is now permitted.

April 2, 1973
Bell Canada
The third inadequacy is the lack of procedures for opposition. I have among my constituents some who would have liked to oppose the application made by the Bell Telephone Company. But the fact that the hearings were being held in Ottawa would have made their appearance very inconvenient and expensive. I understand, also, that the proceedings at pre-hearing conferences were not made available free to intervenors, and this, too, would constitute a financial hardship. In this respect, there is a proposal in the green paper which should be adopted as soon as possible. It reads, and I quote from page 14:
The complexity of the subject and the contingent requirement for highly specialized legal and economic skills have inhibited individuals and groups from appearing before the regulatory board to press their views. The government is accordingly considering a number of suggestions with regard to the representation of consumer interests when licensing and regulatory matters are being dealt with by the Minister of Communications and the federal regulatory bodies.
There is surely a need in this area which must be met speedily by the government. Such a body could also act as an appeal board to consider representations from aggrieved users of the telecommunications system.
In sum, the point is not so much that the decision of the CTC is wrong as that it does not appear to the public that the decision has been made by the most appropriate body, nor does it appear that it has been made in accordance with procedures which allow for sufficient public participation. Just or not, the decision has not been seen to be just.
Perhaps the present problem will force us speedily to adopt the proposals which the minister has placed before us in the green paper.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 COMMUNICATIONS BELL CANADA-RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past several weeks the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) has on several occasions been asked to intervene in the Bell Canada rate hearings on behalf of the public interest and the minister has consistently refused to do so on the ground that the cabinet had the power to disallow a decision of the CTC. It is on this basis that our party is asking the government not to permit the rate increase to be proceeded with pending a thorough review by the cabinet, a review which the minister has already acknowledged lies within the power of the administration.
The minister laid considerable stress this evening upon the fact that the Bell judgment had only been made public at the end of last week. Mr. Speaker, it does not take more than a few moments to recognize that there is considerable public dissatisfaction with the judgment, and it does not need much imagination to undertake to suspend the effects of that judgment until a review can be carried out.
I submit that the arguments put forward by the minister do not detract in any way from the force of the representations and requests made by members of this party.
I was more impressed by some of the arguments put forward by the parliamentary secretary. Extracts have been quoted from the green paper on communications policy. I, too, wish to quote from this document. On page nine we find the following:
Equally important is the fact that efficient low-cost telephone service has come to be looked on as a necessity of life for individual members of the public.

I suggest that this paragraph might well serve as a theme for the debate tonight. What we are concerned with tonight is trying to debate whether such an efficient, low cost service is being provided to the public by Bell Canada; and if there is any doubt about the matter, we say that the cabinet should intervene, make an assessment on behalf of the public and arrive at an objective judgment which, in the words of the parliamentary secretary, may be seen to be just.
If one compares the rates of Bell Canada with those of, say, telephone companies in other provinces-I refer particularly to the western provinces-one will discover in virtually every case Bell rates are substantially higher at the present time despite the fact, one might assume, that Bell enjoys economies of scales which other telephone companies do not. For that reason I suggest there is serious doubt as to whether Bell is offering the kind of low cost, efficient telephone service which the government itself recognizes as a necessity for individual Canadians.
I think what is at issue in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is the ability, or the willingness, of the transport commission to represent the public interest in the hearings which have taken place over a number of years. I think it is instructive to recall that Bell Canada has frequently made application for rate increases down through the years, and the fact is that on no occasion, in all its appearances before the Canadian Transport Commission, has Bell Canada been refused an over-all increase in the rates it charges the public; this in spite of the fact that in its early years Bell exceeded the permissive level of earnings set by the board. I suggest that because of this, in very real measure the transport commission has lost the confidence of the public to act in what it believes to be its best interests.
Moreover, it was frequently recorded during past months that the complexity of the argument which only Bell, I submit, really understood, which Bell designed and which took place on Bell's terms, prevented most if not all of the intervenors being able to make their case satisfactorily. I submit that even the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec publicly conceded that they were unable to present the kind of evidence and to marshall the kind of resources, with the time at their disposal, that would enable them to counter the deep and complex financial rationalizations being put forward by Bell Canada.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the methods of proceeding under which the commission conducts the hearings into Bell Canada applications appear to be designed, as the parliamentary secretary admits, to encourage non-participation on the part of individuals and organized groups alike. What was intended as a quasi-judicial regulatory agency has become, in reality, the playground of the legal profession.
Mr. Speaker, on a number of occasions, through the minister and directly to the commission, requests were made for the commission to facilitate intervention and an expression of opinion by the public. But the commission would not undertake to hold hearings outside the city of
April 2, 1973

Ottawa and, as has already been admitted, many individuals and groups simply were unable to afford the time or the financial resources to appear to present their case.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the public interest was, in large measure, not represented by any agency of this government or this parliament before the hearings of the CTC. It was left-I think this is a matter of regret for members to note-to the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, with such resources and time as they had at their disposal, to represent the public interest.
There have been a number of quotations from the green paper to the effect that the government will be proposing a new regulatory agency to deal with these applications in the future. I submit to this House that the fact that such proposals are being made underlines the weakness of the kind of scrutiny which the CTC has in the past been able to bring to bear upon these applications. If, in fact, the CTC was doing the job properly there would be no need for the minister to stand before us and say, "We are making some changes in the near future." I submit those changes cannot be allowed to take place some months hence. The reasons which gave rise to the need for changes should be brought to bear upon the current applications, for the same reasons as those for which the government now concedes reform is necessary in regulating rate increases of public utilities. For those reasons the cabinet should now undertake to bring scrutiny to bear upon the Bell rate increases. Therefore, I submit that the government's own arguments, couched in its proposals for a new communications policy, in themselves cast doubt upon the commission's ability to adjudicate fairly, objectively and in the public interest the application presented by Bell.
Mr. Speaker, this is, I concede, a complicated subject. One could for some time quote figures in support of one's case. But this is not the time nor the place to repeat all the technical arguments. The point is this: however successfully Bell may have mesmerized the transport commission, its case before the Canadian public has not been proven. Putting it charitably, there exists serious doubt that the rate increases are justified.
I hope that the government takes seriously its responsibility to represent and defend the public interest, as I submit the commission has failed to do. This is a time of mounting and justifiable anxiety about price increases in Canada. In the circumstances, the government is surely obliged to suspend, at least, the implementation of these rate increases pending a thorough review. That review, Mr. Speaker, must place the public interest ahead of Bell Canada's interests. If this happens, I am confident that the government can come to no conclusion other than that the rate increases must not and shall not be proceeded with.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 COMMUNICATIONS BELL CANADA-RATE INCREASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, due to the exclusive monopoly exercised by Bell Canada in Quebec, that province is particularly and severely affected by the rate increase as a result of the fourth application since 1969. This increase soon gave rise to a reaction among Quebecers followed by general dissatisfaction, especially in certain groups affected such as senior citizens, disabled persons, the poor and the tenants.
Bell Canada
Consequently, I feel it is my duty to speak during a few minutes on the motion of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis).
I admit that I am convinced that the cause we are pleading is justified, but when I realized that I was supporting the hon. member for York South, I was somewhat reluctant. I wondered whether I actually was on the right side. But when I found out, after reading his motion, that this would not result in a blame or a non-confidence motion, then, I understood why the hon. member for York South could criticize Bell Canada cheerfully and bravely, with honour and vigour, casually chide the government, because the latter will not be defeated as a result of this debate.
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of using the same language as the hon. member for York South as regards Bell Canada. First of all I would like to clear up a few jurisdictional points and take up again some of the arguments put forward by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier).
The minister indicated that it was impossible for the government to take action at this time and meet our demand that the judgment made by the CTC be suspended, because the autonomy of these quasi-judicial bodies has to be respected. The minister seemed to be sad and unhappy that we called upon him to intervene. He said: Do not call upon me to interfere.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that we do not ask the government to intervene in the course of a hearing by a body. We are only urging the government to take action, to prove its leadership and simply suspend a judgment which has already been made. For what purpose? Because it is a matter of common knowledge that all parties must be heard before a court. Well, before this very decision was made, Bell Canada was one of the only parties to be heard. The public at large never had any opportunity of coming before the court, of setting forth their viewpoint, and of stating that in view of the rising cost of living, for instance, it is impossible for them to agree with the increase that the CTC has just approved.
Consequently, it would only be the most elementary justice to suspend this decision for a moment in order to enable the government, the governor in council, to review the case to ensure that justice has really been done, that all aspects have indeed been weighed in the light of the social context because it is clear to everyone that this fourth or fifth increase in rates is socially unacceptable.
This is why the government would not make an error by interpreting with generosity its jurisdiction under the law, to fulfill the wish of all hon. members and to suspend the decision of the commission. Moreover, it is natural that in the final stage the government become the superior court before which the Canadian people can plead their case through hon. members.
Before ordinary courts, one can be assured that justice will be done because there is always a court of appeal and above it the Supreme Court. But here there is no court beyond the decision of the commission except the one of the Governor general in council that Parliament has wanted to establish under the law. I say to the hon. minister that the first argument does not seem to be very

April 2, 1973
Bell Canada
valuable and I answered with the explanations I have just given.
The second argument used by the minister, and without too much conviction, I must admit, nor too much persuasion, was that they would have to make within two or three days an exceptional decision that an independent board or body could have made in two months. But what is extraordinary about that? Courts do that every day. Courts make decisions within 15 minutes whenever injunctions, for instance are required from the Superior Court and are turned down afterwards. An appeal can be lodged immediately with the appeal Court and immediately the judges for the sake of justice, agree to suspend, to stay the ease, until they have had enough time to make a judgment upon the merits in order to prevent any injustice. Here again, I believe the example applies in the case of the government and it would probably be wise for the government to accept at this time to stay the decision pending further consideration. That is not to prejudge in any way the final decision and neither to criticizing the one that was made. It is simply to show broad-mindedness and wait so that better justice be done to Canadian citizens.
Concluding his speech, the minister said: but there should be a serious reason for me to act. That serious reason, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that it lies in that request for an increase in rates that was granted, which is socially unacceptable and comes as a coicidence-which is quite revealing-at a time when a House committee on the cost of living had to make public a majority report in which they recommended the setting up of a commission to control the cost of living. And in the minority report, we told the government to go further and to implement, among other things an immediate price and wage freeze.
That is an indication that it is not a mere coincidence that this motion is being debated in this House; it is because at the present time the great concern is about the cost of living which has gone beyond bounds, and that concern cannot be allowed to continue. The government must bring in measures and show it is capable of making decisions. That is what we are asking of the government now, and we take the opportunity offered by this debate to say to the government: Set the minds of the people of Canada at rest and as far as this decision is concerned, which must necessarily be of an inflationary nature, postpone it for a while. When you have examined it in depth, when you have allowed the people of Canada to express their views, you may decide as you see fit. But take a decision right now.
Mr. Speaker, now that I have answered some of the arguments made by the Minister of Communications I would like to conclude by saying first of all that Bell Canada deserves to be congratulated. That company undoubtedly deserves it. For years it has succeeded in developing its means of research, showed a sound administration practice made progress in marketing and other fields and that is why that company is recognized throughout the world as a model. We must congratulate Bell for that. But congratulating it does not mean that it is always right. And we submit that in this case it is not right. We submit that the record indicates very clearly that its need for expansion and its quest for reinvestment

are not warranted in the present economic and social context and if that company is not right in this regard we urge the government to be logical and decide on the basis of the general context of the Canadian economy. That increase in rates granted to Bell Canada will become more and more generalized in other fields and will thus become dramatic. The cost of living will become too heavy a burden for the underpriviledged and for middle class people who are too often forgotten.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all be permitted to correct at least one point of the remarks of the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner). To tell the truth, I was somewhat at a loss to understand whether he was for or against but I noticed that he based his first argument on an assertion which I believe to be wrong. He mentioned the lack of participation of ordinary citizens, of intermediary bodies, of anyone other than Bell Canada representatives, at the public hearings held from January 10 to February 16 last whereas, to my knowledge, the number of representations made at that public hearing is the greatest the company has ever received.
Having said that, I was most interested in some of the problems outlined by my colleagues, without going into details, and for good reasons. I believe, for instance, that there are highly specialized technical problems involved. I am thinking of the legal problems, notably the precise nature of the CTC's relations with the cabinet and with Parliament, and the problems of taxation, such as the reviewing of the concept of deferred taxation and its implementation. I am also thinking of administrative problems, such as the quality and quantity of personnel in the Canadian Transport Commission or the administrative plan for the running of the Commission.
For my part, I do not mean to speak on these points, which have already been commented on in outline. I intend to give voice to some more general considerations, for the good reason that since the Commission's decision was only published on Friday, I have not been able to study the decision, or the complete file, for that matter.
Besides that, it seems clear to me that our role as parliamentarians is rather to suggest ideas or basic principles. Here again, I differ from the previous speaker, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, for if I understand correctly, we are soon going to be controlling and reviewing all personal and corporative decisions that are made in Canada. This is really not the role I see myself in, or ourselves. My role is to put forth basic principles, and to enlighten the matter to the best of my knowledge, rather than to get carried away from reading press clippings or extracts taken out of context from just one of the briefs submitted at the public hearing last January and February.
I am not concerned, therefore, with reducing the scope of the debate until we are arguing about dotting the i's and crossing the t's, but rather with reflecting in the name
April 2, 1973

of my constituents on some of the wider aspects of this discussion that affects every family in Canada.

To my way of thinking, it is much too easy to choose a big public corporation such as Bell Canada and make it the villain. That attitude, to me, is by analogy very similar to the one adopted last week by another opposition party which for hours and hours deliberately exploited human misery.

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, except for its shareholders, who likes big corporations? Unless I am mistaken, it is not very profitable these days to be a Bell Canada shareholder. Personally, I do not like paying bills any more than you all.
I have many other reasons however, for complaining about Bell Canada. In my riding, and here I refer to a situation in the metropolis of Canada and not in the Arctic, there still are party lines, and not because people have chosen to use them: there are so many other kinds of entertainment in Montreal.
It seems to me that the fundamental problem of maintaining service rates and facing increased costs of corporation debts, versus an increase in subscribers' rates and the cost of equity should be studied exhaustively.
This being said, the fact remains that as far as I know the quality and the variety of the services offered to Canadians by Bell Canada are outstanding.
A little while ago, as I was listening to the honourable member for York South (Mr. Lewis), I wanted to ask him if he remembered the time when he was a student in Paris. Of course I am a generation remote from him, but nevertheless we have certainly encountered the same problems. He must certainly recall the telephone slugs that you have to buy in each restaurant and that cannot even be used in another telephone booth. I am also thinking about the calls you have to make three or four hours before you can get the connection. As to residents, I think about the months and years they must remain on a waiting list before getting a telephone, without mentioning the basic installation cost of some $500 that the ordinary citizen must pay, and all the rest.
It remains that Bell Canada offers one of the best services in the world, at one of the most reasonable and controlled prices in the world. What can we do?
I imagine that a certain party will answer: Nationalize Bell Canada! and I would understand to some extent! Everybody would want the increases that are paid Bell Canada, the increases which I pay, that is the investments that I offer the company would allow us to be come shareholders at least. Perhaps but would that guarantee a better service at lower cost? Certainly hon. members will allow me to doubt it!
In fact, what is the price of something all about? It seems to me that it is the actual number of hours during which the consumer has to work in order to be in a position to obtain goods or services. Certainly, at the present time, I am not sufficiently briefed to supply figures; no one among us really is.
Bell Canada
However, I think that we should think about that and see that, all things being equal, the portion of the family budget devoted each month to payment of Bell Canada bills has noticeably diminished as compared with what it was 10 or 15 years ago.
However, some questions remain unanswered. One can wonder whether the parallel is fair between the increases in rates obtained by Bell Canada through last Friday's decision and the increase in the cost of living, whether both are commensurate, if I may say so. One may wonder whether the commission is in a position to study the expansion priorities that Bell Canada has set forth itself.
One can wonder whether the act and regulations governing the Canadian Transport Commission can really allow a clear interpretation of the notion of public interest.
All of those questions appear to me much larger than the sole decision of Friday last, that is, rate increases that are not at all agreeable to us; last night I wrote my cheques to the order of Bell Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is surprising to find one of our members so young and attractive, yet so endowed with the principles of "Mother Bell" and tradition that she can see fault in the minor resolution that the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) brought forward today. Obviously, the Canadian people are thinking about nationalization and government control not only of Bell but of all the other telephone companies and communications media in Canada.
It is no longer an advantage to have a telephone; it is a downright necessity, an essential part of life. I would suggest to some of those who question whether the CTC has made the proper judgment to consider the fact that an announcement will be made of the payment in April of a quarterly dividend which will be increased to 71 cents a share. The annual rate will be $2.85 cents a share. Previously, Bell telephone paid three quarterly dividends of 66 cents and one dividend of 67 cents, for an annual rate of $2.65 a share.
What they asked for when they came before the CTC was the right to raise enough money to make an expenditure of $590 million. Leaving aside the fact that they paid this dividend, their shareholders were not too enthusiastic about the stock. As I said, last year they paid a dividend of $2.65. However, the interesting thing is that all they are going to ask for in the financial markets is an additional $200 million in order to raise the $590 million they say is necessary for construction.
Do the members of this House not know what Bell Canada is? Do they not know that they own many subsidiaries in other fields which are also involved in the decision to allow an increase in rates for the service so the corporation can continue to build an empire which is not only in the telephone field? To the best of my knowledge, Northern Electric is still a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bell. It is interesting to note that at no time was the Canadian Transport Commission able to separate what

April 2, 1973
Bell Canada
Bell telephone was making from its own operations, and what they were making from Northern Electric; what they were bleeding off into Northern and how they were making their sales. The CTC spent years trying to find that out, but to my knowledge they have never been able to do so.
I am sure that the CTC is much less competent than was the old board of transport commissioners. It is interesting, however, that Bell telephone also owns other subsidiaries, such as Microsystems International, Nevron Industries Company, Northern Electric Distribution, Northern Electric tele-something, which is in Turkey-even the bilingual members of the House would not able to pronounce that name-and Northern Telecom Inc., in Boston, Massachusetts. It also owns 49 per cent of Bell Northern Research and it owns Northern Telephone in northern Ontario and Northern Telephone in northern Quebec. It owns a vast network of telephone systems.
It may be true that Bell telephone has done an excellent job in the telecommunications field, and I would be the first to admit it. But I suggest that this field is important enough to the people so that even the minister, inept as he may be, has suggested that the government proposes to merge the functions of the Canadian Radio-Television Commission with those of the Canadian Transport Commission which apply to telecommunications carriers, subject to federal regulatory authority. Why is that? Obviously, he has suddenly come to the conclusion that the money people pay for telephone service is not all going into producing telephones or bringing the service up to date; much of it is going into non-allied fields.
We should be interested in looking at some of the figures in relation to the rates paid for telephone service. The figures which I can quote were provided in a Canadian Press survey published in the Gazette on February 15 of this year. They indicate the monthly basic rates for privately-owned telephones in communities with 5,000 to
10,000	telephones. In Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, the rate is $5.60; in Caraquet, New Brunswick, it is $5.10; in Exeter, Ontario, it is $4.50; in Powell River, British Columbia, it is $4.70. But the government-owned telephone system in Flin Flon, Manitoba, is $3.25. This is only about half the cost in some other communities. In North Battleford, Saskatchewan, unlike Glace Bay where it is $5.60, the rate is $3.45- over $2 less. In Lloydminster, Alberta, it is $3.80. This is the rate for government-owned telephones in Alberta, where I have not heard anybody sound remotely as if they would want to nationalize or socialize any kind of public utility.

speechtext:
Few people in Canada today, except for the dinosaurs in political thought, believe that in a monopolistic, public utility company there should be no government ownership or no government control. Our telephone systems now are satellites and are connected through microwave systems to people in every part of the world. It seems to me that this is a sufficiently important segment of our economy to be brought under the control of the people.
It may be that if we are to maintain the standard that we have maintained in telephone communications, not only in Bell telephone but in other telephone systems in Canada-and there are 30 to 40 such systems-we will have to pay more. As the hon. member for Saint-Hyacin-the (Mr. Wagner) said, the cost of living is going up and therefore it is reasonable to expect telephone rates to go up also. But if that is so, at least let us ensure, on behalf of the individual who is paying the bill, that he is getting the most for his money and that he knows to what other uses his money is being put.
Therefore, I suggest that we do not need another "senate" to look after the "senate" that we have created in the CTC, where we put tired, worn-out or defeated politicians.
We need to establish a Crown corporation which will operate our public utility from coast to coast to ensure that not only is it the best possible but that service can be provided to every part of the country through our communications media whether radio, television, telephone or any new developments that take place. That will happen at a cost the people can afford only if we do it publicly, and if we do it all across the country by uniting Bell telephone with all the other systems in Canada, making it a government-operated Crown corporation in the monopoly, public utility field.
