speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me we could sum up the very excellent speech of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) by saying that the essence of it was that the bell tolls for Bell, if he could have his way. It is fascinating, however, to recall that the President of the Canadian Transport Commission, who actually sat on this particular hearing, is the same distinguished gentleman who, as minister of finance, started the inflationary spiral in this country, or at least did more than any other minister of finance to keep it going. How-
April 2, 1973

ever, we now find him, as president of this commission, still pouring oil to fuel the fires of inflation. We are concerned about this. We are very concerned about it. We have shown our concern in our discussions, speeches and questions.
Just today I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what I thought was a very reasonable question. I asked him if he would make a statement on motions as to whether or not the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was stating government policy when he indicated that in his view only the provincial governments had the authority and the jurisdiction to do anything about instituting a freeze or controls on prices. I asked the Prime Minister also if in his statement on motions he would say what, in his opinion, would be an emergency which would prompt the government to act. All we got was a smart-aleck reply, saying that this was asking for a legal opinion. I was not asking him for a legal opinion. If I wanted a legal opinion I would go to a man who knows the law. I would not go to the Prime Minister. I would not go to anybody over there on the other side. In fact I would call them, as we used to call a judge in our county, Judge Necessity. He was called that because we all know how much law necessity knows.
What worries me is the futility of this proceeding today. Here we are with a serious problem facing millions of people in this country and we cannot do anything about it. I give credit to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) for instituting this proceeding so that we can at least do a little talking about it. But this is the House of Commons, this is parliament, and we should have the right to come here and indicate by a recorded vote what we think about the situation.
We are deprived of that opportunity. Why are we deprived of it? It is because hon. gentlemen opposite, or their predecessors, combined with my hon. friends to my left and voted against the amendment to which the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) referred, by means of which we attempted to reserve to the House of Commons some overseeing role with regard to issues of this kind. I can recall that when speaking on behalf of that motion I said, as reported on page 11392 of Hansard for December 20, 1966:
The scope of this act-
That is the National Transportation Act.
-is enormous, and equally vast will be the overriding supervisory authority of the transport commission. Let there be no doubt that if this bill is passed without any material change we shall have surrendered to those men who will compose the commission almost complete authority over a variety of subject matters in the field of transportation which so deeply affects every Canadian and every part of Canada.
It was on that basis that we pursued our course in this debate. The motion was put. The hon. Mr. Pickersgill, at that time the minister in charge of the bill, said the motion had some merit, but, that there were reasons why he did not want to vote for it. The then hon. member for Selkirk, now the Premier of Manitoba, spoke in that debate before the supper hour and said he would support the motion. But obviously, as a young member, he was called by his party leader and told the facts of life. He came back to the chamber after supper and said he would not support the motion. When it was put to a vote members of the party
Bell Canada
opposite and the socialists to my left voted against it, and it was not passed.
If it had been passed there would now be in existence a committee in this parliament charged with the responsibility of scrutinizing the decisions of boards of this kind, and more specifically a decision of this kind. I do not expect, I do not want and I do not believe, that parliament can get into the detail of the decision making process, but when parliament does as it has been doing, to my sadness over the years, gradually divesting itself of all authority to check, challenge and scrutinize the actions of these boards, then, Sir, when motions of this kind come before the House I must recall the sad mistake in judgment made by my hon. friends to my left.
The hon. member for Timiskaming finished his speech by saying, let us create another Crown corporation. That is the only solution the socialists have-create more bureaucracy, more Crown corporations. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain said something about infallibility. The semi-socialists opposite and the socialists to my left seem to believe that all Crown corporations are, in fact, an immaculate conception. I do not believe that. I think they are composed of men and women, dedicated, serious men and women, but that in the final analysis only parliament, and particularly this House, really can deal with the public interest. We may be slow. We may talk too much. You, Mr. Speaker, will probably accept that. We may be clumsy and awkward, but in the final analysis only the House of Commons, elected as it is, has the interests of the people of Canada at heart, and it is for us to make the final decision. That is the problem we face now.
If this motion which I had proposed, and which was referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, had been passed, this committee would now be in existence. We would have been able, by a simple order of the House, to have had the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission referred to that committee for consideration, not in the sense that we would go into all of the technical details but that we, representing the public interest, would have had an opportunity to examine the decision, to call witnesses, and to test the validity, the accuracy and the rightness of the decision. After that, we could have made a report to the House, and the House could have voted on it. The decision of the House would then have been supreme and nobody else, not the CTC and not the government-which isn't a government, which is a Prime Minister surrounded by yes-men-

house with the New Democratic Party trying to offer for

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of the chance to say a few words on this motion. Unlike some opposition members, I am going to try and tell the House clearly whether I am for or against this motion, rather than just making the government bear the brunt of a decision with which they had nothing to do.
I think that the purpose of the motion introduced by the member for York South (Mr. Lewis) is in itself quite praiseworthy, inasmuch as he would like the government to look into the Canadian Transport Commission's decision on the matter of Bell Canada's application "A". I agree in principle, and so, I think, do most Canadians.
I think everyone here will agree that this decision came as a surprise to everyone, and to me more then anyone.
No one expected the Canadian Transport Commission to give their approval to over 80 per cent of the contents of application "A" as presented to them by Bell Canada.
And so it is quite understandable that telephone users are concerned-and rightly so, you have to admit-about this decision and about the rate increases which they will have to put up with.
Now, although I agree with the general principle of the motion, I cannot agree with the way it has been drawn up, because it calls for the implementation of the decision to be suspended immediately; that is where I differ from the member for York South. The same member who was telling us just now that the government cannot act now, that the government will need time to consider thoroughly the CTC's decision, is asking us in the same breath, in his motion, to suspend immediately, and therefore blindly, this same decision. This is where I no longer agree with the motion.
The government will surely need several weeks, if not a month-judging by the discussion I had this afternoon with an official-to consider this decision seriously and give a sound ruling. The CTC took two months to give birth to this baby: a month for the hearings and a review of the briefs submitted, and another month in camera to study and reach the decision it then announced.
Let us not ask the government, after three days, to rule immediately and to suspend, blindly, without knowing whether they are justified in doing so, the decision of the CTC. To my mind, the government would need at least a month to reach a final decision; and at least a week or a week and a half will be required before the Minister of Communications, (Mr. Pelletier) can advise the House of whatever he intends to do.
Why a month's delay? Because one month will be required if the points under dispute and the heart of the matter are to be dealt with, if a rational decision is to be reached. It is not enough to say, "Costs have gone up, leading to inflation". The points under dispute must be clearly identified and to my mind, there are three of them: the first and most important, is the quality of the service.

We probably have in North America the best telephone communications service in the whole world.
I shall not repeat what the hon. member for Saint-Mich-el (Miss Begin) said when she spoke about telephone service in Europe. All those who travel know the low quality of service in continental Europe; they know the waiting periods of an hour or even two hours to put citizens in communication in the same urban center and they know it is sometimes necessary to wait several hours or even till the next day to communicate with someone who lives IOC miles away.
In Canada, we enjoy a service which is far superior to what people have in the other countries. In fact, we can say that there are two kinds of telephone service on earth: the service we have in North America and the one we encounter everywhere else. It is as simple as that.
I think that Canadians have a right to enjoy this service, particularly when one considers that they now get it at a rate which is far cheaper than what European consumers and users pay for a much inferior service. The first disputable point is the quality of service.
The second point, which goes along with the quality of service, is the study of the costs of this service, namely, to see whether the costs are normal for the service the users get. There lies the whole question. It is not simply a matter of saying: prices have increased but of seeing if the increase is warranted, keeping in mind the excellent service we enjoy.
Finally, another point worth studying is the financial situation of Bell Canada. Several hon. members, as a rule those of the New Democratic Party, are always ready to raise a hue and cry on corporations, to say they make too many profits. However, I think that before talking like that, it would be a good thing if the government would seriously examine the financial situation of Bell Canada in order to know if its request for a rate increase is really justified. The government will be able to take realistic and considered measures because if they acted this evening, probably pleasing opposition members, these people would be the first to criticize us in a month or two if it appeared, after a serious study, that the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission was justifiable.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the hon. member is taking so much interest in the company. If the company processes the increase in its computer, and if the
April 2, 1973

government decides that the company must undo what it has done, that is the company's problem. It is asking for the increase. If that increase is not justified, it should suffer for its decision in asking for an increase.

Now, Mr. Speaker, may I continue my remarks.
What is wrong with the resolution, in my opinion, is the request for immediate suspension, as I said, of the Canadian Transport Commission decision. I am in favour of suspension after some time, when it is definitely deemed advisable but a suspension based on clearly unsubstantiated representations of the opposition would seem absurd and unrealistic.
No opposition speaker has mentioned quality or cost of services; none mentioned the various points in support of Bell Canada's application "A". Of course,' the case has just become public, and opposition members know no more about it than the government does at this time. Actually, what is the opposition trying to achieve tonight? The purpose is to bring up the subject of inflation in an effort to convince citizens that the government will be responsible for price increases. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) told us earlier that Mr. Benson, the present Chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, started spiraling inflation and is attempting to perpetuate it through this decision rendered by the Commission. As for the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), he was dissatisfied because the New Democratic Party did not word the motion to blame the government. Come on now! To condemn this government for a decision rendered not by. it but by an independent body is not reasonable.
What they are trying to do tonight is to accuse the government and blame it for this increase, while everybody realizes that this does not make sense. In fact, they seem to be playing political games with this and finally, all that they manage to do, on either side of the House, is to express doubts as to the merits of a decision made by the Canadian Transport Commission. In fact, I understand that doubts may be felt, but let them not ask the government to act immediately on the basis of a doubt. They must realize that this government must take a few days or weeks in order to make a serious decision. I do not think that the people expect a responsible government to show less seriousness. And any government that would act on the basis of a doubt would not enjoy the confidence of the people.
This is why I recommend to this government to take all the time required in order to review the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission.

Bell Canada
decision must be brought to the attention of the government.
I am satisfied that the government will take the necessary steps to examine the reasons which have incited an hon; member to introduce this motion and the points which have been made in support of it. I will merely quote two excerpts of briefs presented by two very representative bodies to the Canadian Transport Commission. First, here are the views of the Canadian Labour Congress:
The Canadian Labour Congress welcomes this opportunity to submit its objections to the last request made by Bell Canada in its application "A" for the approval of its proposed adjustments in its rates related to services, equipment and facilities. Such application, if it were agreed to, would bring to this company, as estimated by itself, additional revenues amounting to $36 million for 1973 . .. We wish however to point out from the outset that the Congress is speaking on behalf of a much wider sector of the population since its concern is not limited to the narrow scope of the union movement. Rather our brief is expressing the frustration and the discontent caused by Bell's off-hand attitude towards individuals and groups, and which have been conveyed to the Congress through letters and private communications. In brief, we are not only the spokesmen of the Congress members in these regions, but we are also quite concerned that the proposed increases will cause additional hardships for the aged, the disabled, the unemployed, pensioners on fixed income and low income people ...
I for one am convinced that the CLC officials did not try to exploit human misery, no more than the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe earlier when he suggested that those people will suffer as a consequence of the increases authorized by the Canadian Transport Commission.
When we mention the serious situation of underprivileged people, I am a little tired of hearing some hon. members accusing us of trying to make cheap political gains and of politicking. I hope this will be taken into account in the future.
At any rate, this is what the CLC thinks-and here I call the attention of the minister upon this so that the government can see whether there was abuse or not and I quote:
During the period from 1958 to the mid-sixties, Bell Canada exceeded the level of earnings allowed by the former Transport Commission. Expressed in actual money earnings, the excess of profits that Bell Canada illegally drew out, in contravention of the commission's order, was approximately $37 million. And as the corporate tax reached an average of 50 per cent at that time, one can say that the Bell succeeded in drawing out $75 million from telephone users through a direct violation of the commission's decision.
That is why I invite the government to watch closely the decisions made by the Canadian Transport Commission and even in the case of an independent body, I think it is up to the government to see that the corporations abide by the decisions that are made and that they do not go beyond the decisions, as was reported in the CLC brief.
Moreover, I am convinced of one thing: a member said a while ago-and I agree with him-that Canada has one of the best telephone services. I admit that Bell Canada had a great part in it, but I also recognize that the company is mainly doing business in the most profitable and advantageous centres. That is why they can make profits.
I can also recall the days when areas had no telephone service and Bell Canada would not provide them with the

April 2, 1973
Bell Canada
necessary service on the grounds that it was not financially sound. Therefore with the help of a few of my fellow-citizens, I worked on setting up a cooperative telephone network and for 20 years I have been the manager of this business. Therefore, I am in a position to speak with some knowledge and state that a telephone company is one of the most profitable things to operate.
Therefore, I feel no pity at all for Bell Canada because they do make profits, and I understand that they have developed into a corporation for this purpose. But there are also limits, and I do believe that because of abuses, the confidence that the public may have in private enterprise is falling short.
The capitalistic system, in my opinion, is good in itself. It is good when it is reasonable. When it becomes faulty and that we try only to recognize and develop the financial capital without taking into account the rights of the human capital, I suggest that the government must interfere in order to set a limit so that the rights of the population are not encroached upon.
A moment ago an honourable member was mentioning the rising cost of living. It is a fact that prices are increasing in almost all areas. We will have to take a decision sometime! We should not allow big, powerful and strong people to increase their prices according to their fancy, and ask the small fellow to be reasonable, to refrain from asking for any increase in wages, to try and be satisfied with whatever he has.
A responsible government must look after the welfare of the people, and I agree that in the case before us, they must be given the necessary time to analyse the whole situation and take a decision without delay in accordance with the common good.
At any rate, my deep thought is the following: Bell Canada is in such a financial position, as I understand, that it may proceed at present with intended developments without having to increase its rates.
These are not paltry increases when you are talking of 50 percent in the case of installation of equipment. I should have been happy to benefit by such increases when I was the manager of the cooperative telephone network I referred to a short while ago. At that time, we were controlled by the Quebec public services Board and when we applied for small increases this resulted in quite a number of hearings, and only after we had demonstrated the necessity for an increase was a decision made to grant it by order.
In the present circumstances, as I said-

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly and unpretentiously during this debate but with the intention of expressing a rather deep conviction.

The debate held this evening is extremely interesting since it gives to all the members the opportunity to take a stand on this matter of public interest. We learned a few days ago that Bell Canada was authorized to increase its rates. I think that all members recognize as I do that the services provided by Bell Canada are comparable to any other offered throughout the world.
Bell Canada is reputed-and I think that such a claim is valid-to be providing services which do credit to all Canadian people. The question raised today is to determine whether the requested increase not only meets the corporation's needs, but if it can provide the necessary funds.
This debate gives me the first opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to take a stand on a basic question, namely that of the action of a political power on a judicial or quasi-judicial body.
Mr. Speaker, ever since 1968 when I had the honour of sitting in this House, I have always been-and there is no secret about it-a stubbornly argued for the division between the judicial or quasi-judicial power and the political power.
This evening I should like to suggest to my colleagues that it is extremely important, as hon. members, to be able to respect the decision of an independent authority which, in this case, is the Canadian Transport Commission which exercises powers that we have freely conferred upon it.
Far be it from me to pretend that this decision which we are discussing meets all the criteria of justice that we would have liked to see in a decision made by an authority in which we vested powers. But I remain convinced, Mr. Speaker, that in the final analysis that decision which was made in good faith by the Commission after an in depth examination of the applications or the arguments submitted to it represents the opinion of a good number of experts who submitted to this House an opinion which I consider undoubtedly as debatable.
I think that if we look at that decision, first of all we are surprised that it authorizes a rather substantial increase in the rates Bell Canada can charge the public. Right off the bat I would be inclined to make a general criticism. It seems to me that the Commission, with all due respect, did not take into consideration the capacity of the public to provide an additional income to that company. With regard to the powers of the Canadian Transport Commission I have to admit that it acted according to its prerogatives and the powers that we, as members of this House, have given it.
However, I am somewhat disappointed that the Commission restricted its action to the powers it had been given. It seems to me that it would have been not only possible but even easy for the Commission to wonder about the capacity of the public to meet those increases in rates.
I think that while recognizing that Bell Canada offers services which are generally better than those provided by other companies of the same size it must be recognized that the public is now grappling with the problems of inflation and the cost of living that is going up at an alarming rate. And if we accept that Bell Canada should consider giving improved services, I think it would have

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently we had the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission in connection with the application by Bell Canada to increase its rates. That decision was made without even the benefit of a white paper. The president of the Canadian Transport Commission gave us, when he was minister of finance, the "glories" of our present Income Tax Act. Now the commission has authorized Bell Canada rate increases which are really suspect. I hope in the few minutes allotted to me to outline some of the suspicions many of us have in connection with these increases. I should like to repeat the promise given to this country by the leader of our party, namely, that he would make sure the present commissioner was returned to his accounting practice so he could enjoy the benefits of the act that he foisted upon the people. As time goes on we will have to develop a proper board system for reviewing prices, not only of companies like Bell Canada but rail rates as well. Prices of other monopolies or quasi-monopolies will have to be reviewed, in the public interest. It is important that a tribunal system be organized so as properly to administer this kind of review.
Our judicial procedures are based upon the adversary system of justice, where an independent tribunal listens to argument presented on one side by a litigant or proposer and to argument presented by those on the other side, and thus arrives at a decision. In matters as complicated as telephone rates, indeed in matters as complicated as freight rates, the public interest cannot be protected by ad hoc representations, even by authorities as powerful as the province of Ontario or the province of Quebec. These matters are so complicated that the public interest must be protected by independent action which presents the public's case to the inquiry, so that the public can draw out, under the light of proper cross-examination and the presentation of relevant facts, what is the true position of the person or corporation that is applying for a rate or price increase. This is a matter the government will have to consider. This is one of the reasons the suggestion that this particular rate increase must be suspended, at least for the present, is valid.
At this point I want to deal with several questions that were raised during the Bell Canada hearing which indicate to me and to others in this House that there is something seriously wrong with the increase awarded. A great deal has been said about modernization of equipment, the cost of expansion of service, the necessity that shareholders receive a fair return on their money, and that investors are induced to lend money to this corporation on the basis that the corporation's charges will justify such investment. I appreciate those remarks, and I think that even the members of the party to my left can understand that obviously this corporation must earn a sufficient return in order to pay its debts and to pay for the use of 26087-371

money at its command. However, I should like to present some matters and questions that occur to me in connection with the decision made by the Canadian Transport Commission.
First of all, this corporation has a quasi-monopoly on television cable distribution in many of our communities. This television cable service is rented to a TV company or cable company for a limited period of time and then the contract can easily be terminated. There is no requirement that the use of Bell facilities can go on and on. Speaking to television cable companies, I am informed that the monopoly aspect of Bell in regard to this service causes serious concern. Secondly, Bell has spent a great deal of money through its many subsidiaries on research and development. This research seems to have been charged to Northern or to one of the other subsidiaries, but really it is charged against the regular telephone cost to every user. There is no question that this research should increase the share value of Bell, and increase it dramatically. Is there any reason why Bell stock is selling for 10, 11 or even 12 times book value? If this company is going to do that through its subsidiary, the research company, then the market should appreciate that research and the value of it, in the long term, should be considered when rate charges are made against regular telephone subscribers of Bell.
It is doubtful whether the commission has looked properly into the relationships that exist between Microsystems International Limited, Nevion Industries Limited, Bell Northern Research Limited, and Bell Northern Telecommunications Inc. Indeed, one columnist suggested that the reason for the increase is Bell's ownership of Anik.
We should also have inquired whether Bell is borrowing its money at the cheapest possible rate in order to conduct the expansion necessary in telecommunications in this country. Perhaps there are other methods by which this corporation could obtain something on a longer term basis or on a lower interest basis, so that the need for increased charges to consumers would not arise.
Thirdly, many of us question how Bell gets away with its fancy Princess phones, its coloured units, its inordinate charges for yellow page advertisements and all sorts of other gimmicks that the company is able to dream up. The real question is whether this company is acting in the national interest.
I am glad the minister is in the chamber, because I want to mention another matter. Last December, Bell-and I wonder how closely the minister has got into bed with Bell-was given a licence in my riding for one of these Bellboy transmission systems. I checked into that system and was told that Bell was supposed to have a 100-watt transmitter. Some of our investigations indicated that Bell was actually transmitting at 400 to 700 watts. When I asked the minister for a copy of Bell's licence, he said, "Oh no; licences are privileged." Members of Parliament are not entitled to look at a Bell transmission licence. So I am given cause to wonder how deeply the minister is in bed with Bell Canada.
During the election campaign the New Democratic Party made great play of capital cost allowances. Did this commission look into the depletion and depreciation rates

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened this evening to the speech of the hon. member for Saint-Michel (Miss Begin) and it sounded much like a speech written by the recently elected president of Bell Canada, Monsieur Grandpre. One of the things that concerned me very much was the statement earlier today that the CTC is an independent body, yet the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested he wanted to get this commission free of political interference and pressure. This seems like a strange position for one to take, considering that the commission was appointed by the government and that its president is a former cabinet member.
In view of the fact that this government does have authority to roll back the rate increases awarded to Bell Canada by the CTC, I think morally the government should do so. After all, which is the most important: the commission appointed by this government, or the elected representatives of the people of Canada? Surely we should decide which is to make the decisions in the public interest.
Bell Canada went before the Canadian Transport Commission to receive approval of its application for rate increases in 1973 and 1974. The CTC should not have granted these rate increases, when we consider the kind of complex questions raised regarding monopolies, profits, service, communications, corporate responsibility and the cost of living.
In the first instance, Bell Canada sought rate increases on the plea of poverty. Their argument was something like this: Profits have risen but they have not risen high enough to satisfy the investors; therefore, the company is encountering increasing difficulties in raising in the money market funds it needs for the capital expansion that must be undertaken.
The figures show that Bell Canada's profit for 1971 was $147 million, up from $108.5 million in 1967. In the last ten years, total profits were $1,021,135,000. Between 1962 and 1971, profits increased by 125.6 percent. It should be noted that Bell Canada has $233.6 million in deferred taxes owing to the Canadian people. According to the publication "Corporations" with a directory of Canada's top 100

companies excluding government-owned corporations, Bell Canada is number one in rank by assets, number one in rank by net income and third in rank by sales.
If the investor is not satisfied with Bell Canada's financial position, what precisely does it take to satisfy him? Should it be the role of the older citizen to pay through the nose for an ordinary telephone service, a public utility, in profit terms, thereby increasing its justification for an over-all telephone rate increase in order to satisfy the investor? I do not think that is right.
This brings me to the issue of what price we should pay for our telephone service. A comparison of telephone rates in other provinces shoes that while people in Ontario and Quebec pay an $11 service charge for the installation of an ordinary, black telephone, Albertans and British Columbians pay $10. In Saskatchewan and Manitoba, where the telephone companies are government-owned, the same service costs $2 to $3. At the same time, the average monthly rate for a phone in Ontario and Quebec is $6.10 but B.C. residents pay $5.55 per month, Albertans pay $3.35, while Saskatchewan subscribers pay $4.15, and Manitobans $3.90.
Keeping in mind these figures, consider that among the many increases Bell has been awarded by the CTC is an increase in the installation charge from $11 to $22, as well as increases in monthly rates and long distance calls, pay phone calls will be doubled to 20 cents and operator assistance will cost 25 cents per call if the number is in the directory.
In theory, the rates of Bell Canada are governed by the people of Canada. But Bell Canada, being a public utility monopoly, is required by law to present an application for rate increases for approval by the CTC, which is a government agency. The public, then, has the right to object to or support the application. Citizen interventions should bear weight with the CTC, yet in 1973 the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, the Association of Ontario Mayors and Reeves, the Ontario Municipal Association, the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and some 200 municipalities in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, among others, made representations against Bell's rate application; and still Bell Canada has had its application approved by the CTC.
The same was true in 1969. For those most severely affected by rate increases-that is, those on fixed incomes, pensioners, the unemployed, low income earners and small businessmen-the difficulties of being adequately represented at rate hearings are virtually insurmountable. It is also intriguing to note that prior to 1969, Bell had made application for a reduction in rates of certain long distance calls. By 1969, however, the figures show that 99 per cent of all households in Ontario and Quebec had acquired telephone service. Then Bell applied for rate increases in 1969, 1970 and 1971, as well as for 1973 and for 1974. Bell is, consequently, now in the position which enables it to make exorbitant demands, secure in the knowledge that few subscribers will give up their telephone and that there is no competing company to whom those in disagreement with rates and service can turn for a telephone.
Although Bell has gone to great pains to justify its application for rate increases, it strains both the public
April 2, 1973

good will and credibility when we look at some of Bell's operations. For instance, the rates we pay for telephones are governed by the rate group in which we live. That rate group is determined by the number of telephones in the area, the number of main phones plus extensions. In other words, the more phones and extensions in the area, the higher the rates. Consider, then, that Bell, in an apparently unprecedented burst of Christmas spirit, offered last November the installation of an extension phone free of charge. Many took advantage, not realizing the cost implications.
Let us consider, as an example, Northern Electric, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bell Canada. It has received $26 million in government grants, plus an effective tax rate of 9.8 per cent, and $14.1 million in deferred taxes; yet that company managed to lay off 5,000 employees in one
Bell Canada
and a half years. In addition, Microsystems International, a Northern Electric subsidiary, received an interest-free loan of $12 million from the federal treasury in July, 1969. In May, 1972, Microsystems announced it had built a new assembly plant in Malaysia and practically at the same time 50 persons were laid off in Ottawa. We must also consider the situation in respect of Tele-Direct, a subsidiary of the same company.
My time is running out. I should like to conclude this speech by saying that I feel the government ought to refute the decision by the CTC, and roll back the increase granted to Bell Canada. Indeed, many people in Nickel Belt would far rather see added to the words on the sign outside the Bell Canada office here in Ottawa, "Place Bell Canada"-"Under public ownership".

Tuesday. April 3. 1973
